textClass.keywords: NEIL1 Temozolomide resistance Glioma Oxidative stress 2-thioxanthine

div.p: Background: Glioma is the most common malignant primary brain tumor. Temozolomide (TMZ) is the standard first-line chemotherapy, but its efficacy is severely limited by acquired resistance. Understanding resistance mechanisms, especially beyond traditional DNA repair, is crucial for improving outcomes. Methods: We integrated multi-database glioma transcriptomics (TCGA, GTEx, CGGA). Bioinformatics (differential expression, WGCNA, glycolipid metabolism gene screening) and machine learning (LASSO, random forest) identified key genes, focusing on the DNA glycosylase NEIL1. Its expression was assessed in U251 MG cells versus TMZ-resistant (U251 MG/TMZ) cells. Gain/loss-of-function studies (lentiviral knockdown/overexpression) and pharmacological inhibition (a 2-thioxanthine derivative, TX16) were used to evaluate NEIL1′s role in proliferation (CCK-8, EdU), migration, invasion, apoptosis (TUNEL), ROS, and TMZ sensitivity (IC50). A subcutaneous nude mouse model provided in vivo validation. Results: NEIL1 was aberrantly expressed in glioma and enriched in PI3K-Akt/cAMP signaling, suggesting that it may promote the malignant behavior of U251 MG cells through these pathways. Its expression was significantly higher in TMZ-resistant cells (P < 0.001). NEIL1 overexpression promoted malignant phenotypes (proliferation, migration, invasion, P < 0.05), while its knockdown suppressed them. Critically, NEIL1 overexpression attenuated TMZ-induced ROS and DNA damage, increased cell viability and IC 50 (1.2-fold), and bolstered TMZ resistance. The NEIL1 inhibitor TX16 reversed these malignant behaviors and restored TMZ sensitivity (P < 0.05), reinstating ROS-driven apoptosis. In vivo, NEIL1 promoted tumor growth, which was suppressed by TX16. Conclusion: NEIL1 drives glioma malignancy and TMZ resistance by mitigating oxidative stress and DNA damage, highlighting its role as a promising target to overcome chemoresistance.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Glioma represents the most prevalent malignant brain tumor affecting the central nervous system. Standard clinical intervention includes maximal surgical excision along with radiotherapy and chemotherapy [1]. Temozolomide (TMZ) remains the predominant first-line chemotherapeutic option [2], attributed to its favorable property of traversing the blood-brain barrier and prolong median survival in patients [3,4]. Nevertheless, approximately half of the patients develop resistance to TMZ, resulting in unsatisfactory therapeutic efficacy and poor overall prognosis [5]. TMZ resistance has become a principal barrier to effective glioma treatment and a major contributor to poor patient outcomes [6,7] Therefore, elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying TMZ resistance and identifying actionable targets are urgent needs in both clinical and basic research.

Among the known resistance mechanisms, activation of DNA damage repair pathways is considered a central factor [8,9]. As an alkylating agent, TMZ induces base mismatches and DNA damage by introducing methyl groups into genomic DNA, primarily at the O⁶-position of guanine, leading to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis [10]. Glioma cells frequently exhibit high expression of O⁶-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT), an enzyme capable of removing such methylation, thereby neutralizing TMZ-induced cytotoxicity and resulting in resistance [11]. Although silencing MGMT renders patients more responsive to TMZ, nearly 50 % of patients still fail to survive beyond two years, and some resistant individuals may exhibit sporadic responses to TMZ therapy, indicating the involvement of additional factors in TMZ resistance [12,13]. Existing studies have shown that metabolic reprogramming plays an important role in TMZ resistance in glioma cells. For example, the long non-coding RNA ZBED3-AS1 can bind to the transcription factor Spi-1, thereby inhibiting glycolysis and reducing TMZ resistance [14]. In addition, inhibition of the circular RNA circKIF4A has been proven to decrease glycolytic flux and significantly enhance TMZ sensitivity [15]. Therefore, investigating the metabolic dimension of TMZ resistance may reveal new avenues to overcome chemoresistance.

NEIL1 (Nei-like DNA glycosylase 1) functions as an essential glycosylase within the base excision repair (BER) system of eukaryotic cells, primarily responsible for recognizing and excising oxidatively damaged bases [16][17][18]. It is vital for preserving genomic integrity and preventing mutational accumulation [19]. Dysfunction of NEIL1 leads to the accumulation of oxidative lesions and elevated mutation rates, increasing the risk of tumorigenesis in tissues such as the stomach and colorectal epithelium [20,21]. Moreover, NEIL1 has been implicated in the regulation of cellular oxidative stress and apoptotic pathways: its enzymatic activity is modulated by intracellular oxidative levels and can enhance cellular tolerance to oxidative damage when required. Upregulation of NEIL1 enzymatic activity in humans has been shown to facilitate the assembly of repair complexes on chromatin, thereby improving resistance to oxidative stress [22]. Another anti-glioma mechanism of TMZ is the induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which triggers mitochondrial damage and promotes apoptosis in glioma cells [23,24]. However, under sustained TMZ pressure, glioma cells undergo significant reprogramming of redox homeostasis. For example, TMZ-resistant cells upregulate the NRF2-GSH/xCT antioxidant axis and related nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH)-producing pathways, thereby rapidly eliminating TMZ-induced ROS, maintaining low oxidative stress, and escaping drug-induced cytotoxicity [25,26]. Therefore, whether NEIL1 plays a role in oxidative stress that contributes to TMZ resistance in glioma cells warrants further investigation. While the role and expression of NEIL1 in glioma remain underexplored, its multifaceted functions in oxidative damage repair, cellular metabolism, and survival signaling suggest a potential influence on the cellular response to TMZ-induced stress.

In conclusion, TMZ resistance remains a major challenge in glioma therapy, involving complex mechanisms such as DNA repair and metabolic reprogramming. In this study, glioma-related clinical datasets were retrieved from public databases such as The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Genotype-Tissue Expression databases (GTEx). Key genes closely associated with glioma were identified using machine learning, integrated analysis of glycolipid metabolism, and survival/prognostic correlation. Ultimately, NEIL1 was selected as a candidate gene of interest. As a critical enzyme for the repair of oxidative DNA damage, NEIL1 exhibits multifunctional roles in regulating cellular stress responses and metabolism. It was found that NEIL1 overexpression suppressed oxidative stress in U251 MG cells, promoted proliferation, migration, and invasion, and enhanced TMZ resistance. These findings offer new theoretical insights into the mechanisms of glioma chemoresistance and may provide novel strategies to improve patient outcomes.

div.head: Dataset acquisition
div.p: In this study, the training data were sourced from TCGA and GTEx, where glioma tissue samples were sourced from TCGA and normal brain tissue samples from GTEx [27,28]. Validation datasets were obtained through the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA) [29]. Additionally, genes associated with glycolipid metabolism were retrieved from the GeneCards (http://www.genecards.org/).

div.head: Differential expression gene (DEGs) analysis
div.p: All tissue samples were categorized into two groups: glioma (Tumor group) and normal control (Normal group). Screening for DEGs was performed with the "Limma" package (3.60.4) in R. Genes satisfying P < 0.05 and |log2 fold change (FC)| > 0.585 were regarded as statistically significant. Volcano plots and heatmaps of the identified DEGs were generated using the "ggplot2" package (3.5.1).

div.head: Identification of key glioma modules using WGCNA
div.p: We applied weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to analyze glioma datasets and clinical parameters [30]. The soft-threshold value was optimized using the "pickSoftThreshold" function to ensure a scale-free topology. Pearson correlation within the adjacency matrix was used to evaluate gene relationships, and weighted connections highlighted critical modules for further study.

div.head: Screening and functional analysis of candidate genes
div.p: To identify critical glioma-related genes, the overlapping genes among DEGs, key WGCNA modules, and glycolipid metabolism-related genes were processed by Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression and Random Forest (RF) analysis. Venn diagrams were created using EVenn (http://www.ehbio. com/test/venn/#/) to identify the intersection of candidate genes from both algorithms. Functional enrichment analysis of the candidate genes was conducted based on annotations from Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) and Gene Ontology (GO) databases. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was capplied based on the C2 collection from the MsigDB database to evaluate pathway enrichment between the two groups, and results with P < 0.05 were deemed significant. Networks linking genes and pathways, together with pathway maps, were built to explore the regulatory functions of candidate genes in glioma progression.

div.head: Feature gene selection via machine learning
div.p: To refine the list of core genes, the "glmnet" package (4.1-8) was applied for LASSO regression, where five-fold cross-validation optimized the penalty parameter. Coefficients were shrunk by the L1 constraint, discarding less informative variables and keeping the most relevant predictors. Subsequently, the "randomForest" package (4.7-1.1) was used to identify genes with the highest Mean Decrease Gini values, indicating their importance.

div.head: Construction and evaluation of glioma prognostic model
div.p: A prognostic risk model for glioma was constructed using datasets from TCGA and GTEx, while the CGGA served as the validation set. Genes commonly identified through both LASSO and RF analyses were analyzed through multivariate Cox regression to identify independent survival-associated markers and generate the risk model. The Cox model evaluated the contribution of each variable to overall survival. The risk score was calculated as follows: Riskscore = Coef(gene1) × Expr(gene1) + Coef(gene2) × Expr(gene2)
where Coef represents the regression coefficient, and Expr corresponds to Z-score normalized expression. Glioma cases were classified into lowand high-risk groups using the median score.

div.head: Construction of nomogram
div.p: To optimize and visualize the clinical utility of the prognostic model, a nomogram was generated through the "rms" package (6.8-2) [31]. Independent prognostic factors identified from the multivariate Cox analysis (gene expression levels) were incorporated into the nomogram to calculate individualized risk scores for each patient. Each variable was assigned a corresponding score on the nomogram, with higher total scores indicating worse prognosis. Calibration curves were used to eassess the predictive performance of the nomogram by comparing predicted and observed survival probabilities. Calibration was performed for 1-year, 1.5-year, and 2-year survival using 1000 bootstrap resampling to ensure robustness. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were conducted through the "survival" (3.7-0) and "survminer" (0.4.9) to illustrate survival differences between risk groups. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and the corresponding area under the curve (AUC) values were derived with the "pROC" package (1.18.5) to evaluate model classification performance.

div.head: Animals
div.p: The method for establishing the subcutaneous xenograft model was conducted as previously described [32]. All animal procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of Shanghai Tenth People's Hospital Hopital (SHDSYY-2024-19,850). Female BALB/c nude mice (6 weeks old) were obtained from Cyagen Biosciences Inc. (Cyagen, USA) and acclimated under specific conditions (25-27 • C, 55 ± 5 % humidity) for one week. Cell suspensions (1 × 10⁷ cells/mL, 20 μL) were injected subcutaneously into the dorsal region of mice. When tumor volume reached 0.1 cm³, TMZ was administered orally (20 mg/kg/day; 5 days/week; 3 cycles) was initiated. Tumor size was measured every 5 days using a caliper, and volume was calculated using the formula: Tumor volume = (a × b²)/2,where a is the longest and b is the shortest diameter. Tumor growth curves were plotted based on volume changes. Tumors were harvested on day 21 for further analysis.

div.head: Synthesis of 2TX derivatives
div.p: According to the procedure reported in the literature, the 2TX derivative was synthesized as follows. 4,5-Diamino-2,6-dithiolpyrimidine was thoroughly mixed with urea and heated in an oil bath. Potassium hydroxide solution was then added to completely dissolve the solidified material. The resulting high-temperature mixture was treated with activated Norit charcoal for decolorization and subsequently filtered.

Concentrated hydrochloric acid was added to acidify the filtrate, and the resulting precipitate was collected, washed with distilled water, and dried under reduced pressure to obtain the TX16 solid. TX16 was dissolved in DMSO and diluted with culture medium or physiological saline. The working concentration for cell experiments was 5 μM, and the working dose for animal experiments administered via intravenous injection was 1 mg/kg/day.

div.head: Lentiviral vector construction
div.p: To achieve stable NEIL1 knockdown and overexpression, lentiviral vectors for NEIL1-nonsense control (NEIL1 NC) , NEIL1-shRNA knockdown (NEIL1 KD ), and NEIL1 overexpression (NEIL1 •E ) were constructed and obtained from Genomeitech (China).

div.head: Fluorescence staining assays
div.p: TUNEL-positive signals were detected using the TUNEL Apoptosis Detection Kit (Beyotime, China) to assess the rate of apoptosis. EdU incorporation was detected using the EdU Cell Proliferation Assay Kit (Beyotime, China) for detecting cellular proliferative activity. Cell nuclei were counterstained with DAPI dye to facilitate nuclear localization. ROS levels were quantified through the Reactive Oxygen Species Assay Kit (Beyotime, China) to determine the extent of oxidative stress. Ki67 expression was evaluated via immunofluorescence staining. Cells were incubated with the Ki67 antibody (CL555-27,309, Proteintech, China) to assess proliferative activity.

div.head: Cell culture
div.p: The human glioma cell line U251 MG was purchased from Beyotime Biotech Inc. and grown in DMEM supplemented with 10 % FBS [33]. The TMZ-resistant cell line U251 MG/TMZ was generated by continuously exposing U251 MG cells to a single high concentration of TMZ over a period of approximately six months [34]. The cells were maintained in medium containing 200 μM TMZ to preserve the resistant phenotype.

div.head: Cellular phenotype assays
div.p: CCK-8 was used to evaluate viability and derive IC50 values. Migration ability was evaluated using the wound-healing assay, calculating the reduction in wound gap. Invasion capacity was determined via Transwell assay, followed by crystal violet staining for visualization and quantification.

div.head: qRT-PCR
div.p: RNA was extracted and reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the Pri-meScript™ RT reagent Kit with gDNA Eraser (Takara, Japan). Quantitative detection of mRNA expression was carried out with TB Green® Premix Ex Taq™ (Takara, Japan). Each sample was tested in triplicate. GAPDH served as the endogenous control. Primers were designed as follows: NEIL1: 5′-AACTAGGATTTGGAGCCTC -3′ and 5′-AGGCGAAGGTGTGCCTTAAGT -3′ GAPDH: 5′-TGTGTCCGTCGTGGaTCTGA -3′ and 5′-TTGCTGTTGAA GTCGCAGGAG -3′. Relative mRNA expression levels of each gene were calculated using the 2 -△△Ct method based on the quantitative Ct values.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: For bioinformatic data, analyses were carried out in R software (4.4.1). For experimental part, data were analysed with SPSS (16.0). Data are shown as mean ± SD for continuous variables, and as counts/ percentages for categorical ones. Comparisons used t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for two groups, and ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis for multiple groups. Chi-squared or Fisher's exact test analyzed categorical data. Survival was assessed by Kaplan-Meier with log-rank test. Model discrimination was estimated using AUC, and DeLong's test compared AUCs. Calibration verified predicted vs observed outcomes. P < 0.05 was considered significant.

div.head: Differential expression analysis of DEGs
div.p: From TCGA and GTEx, 702 glioma and 1152 control samples involving 11,701 coding genes were analyzed. 1339 DEGs were detected, comprising 599 genes significantly upregulated and 790 significantly downregulated in glioma samples (Fig. 1).

div.head: WGCNA and identification of key modules
div.p: Gene expression data from TCGA and GTEx were analyzed by WGCNA to detect modules associated with glioma traits. First, scale-free topological networks were constructed using different soft-threshold powers. The scale-free topology fit index R² was evaluated under various power values (Fig. 2A). When the soft threshold reached 9-10, R² approached 0.9 for the first time, and was therefore selected as the candidate threshold. Further analysis showed that average connectivity decreased as the soft threshold increased (Fig. 2B). A soft-threshold power of 9 was ultimately selected as it offered a saturated R² value and acceptable mean connectivity. A gene dendrogram and module eigengene similarity heatmap were then generated (Fig. 2C-D). The heatmap illustrating the correlations between gene modules and clinical traits (normal and glioma groups) was constructed (Fig. 2E). The modules most positively correlated with glioma were MEturquoise (r = 0.98, P = 1e-220), MEpurple (r = 0.66, P = 4e-231), and MEpink (r = 0.65, P = 1e-223), suggesting that the genes in these modules could be pivotal in the onset and advancement of tumors. A scatter plot illustrating the correlation between module membership (6064 genes in MEturquoise) and significance with the tumor group was further presented (Fig. 3).

div.head: Screening and functional analysis of candidate genes
div.p: To further identify glioma-related candidate genes, a set of metabolismrelated genes, particularly those involved in glucose metabolism, was included. The intersection of DEGs, MEturquoise module members, and glucose metabolism-related genes resulted in 394 overlapping genes (Fig. 4A-B). These genes were subjected to functional enrichment analyses. GO enrichment results (Fig. 4C) revealed that, in the Biological Process (BP) category, genes were significantly enriched in "mitotic sister chromatid segregation", "nuclear division", and "nuclear chromosome segregation", all of which are closely related to cell proliferation, division, and organ development. In the Cellular Component (CC) category, genes were mainly enriched in "collagen-containing extracellular matrix", "membrane raft", and "sarcomere", suggesting their involvement in structural and adhesionrelated functions. In the Molecular Function (MF) category, significant enrichment was observed in "iron ion binding" and "extracellular matrix structural constituent", indicating roles in signal transduction, molecular binding, and structural integrity. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis (Fig. 4D) showed significant involvement of these genes in multiple signaling pathways related to proliferation, migration, and metabolic regulation, including the "PI3K-Akt signaling pathway", "ECM-receptor interaction", and "cAMP signaling pathway". Additionally, enrichment in the "AGE-RAGE signaling pathway in diabetic complications" indicated participation in metabolic disease-related stress responses. GSEA was further employed to reveal functional characteristics of the differential genes. The results demonstrated significant enrichment in gene sets closely related to proliferation, transcriptional regulation, and tumor progression, including NUYTTEN_EZH2_TARGETS_DN, FLORIO_NEOCORTEX _BASAL_RADIAL_GLIA_DN, FISCHER_DREAM_TARGETS, and SHEDDEN_-LUNG_CANCER_POOR_SURVIVAL_A6 (Fig. 4E-F). These gene sets displayed high Normalized Enrichment Scores (NES) and significant P-values, suggesting that the identified genes may occupy central positions in known proliferation-associated pathways. The pathway-gene association network (Fig. 4G) revealed that multiple pathways were enriched for a core group of highly overlapping genes, such as MYC, BIRC5, TOP2A, CDK1, and TPX2, indicating their coordinated involvement in the regulation of the cell cycle and malignant progression across diverse signaling cascades. Furthermore, a pathway-pathway interaction network (Fig. 4H) demonstrated significant gene overlaps among enriched pathways, forming distinct functional clusters. Strong interconnections were especially observed among cancer subtype pathways associated with proliferation, differentiation, and prognosis, reinforcing the central regulatory roles of these candidate genes in tumor phenotypes.

div.head: Feature gene selection via machine learning
div.p: To further refine glioma-related feature genes, two machine learning algorithms were introduced: LASSO regression and RF. First, the optimal value of λ was determined via 5-fold cross-validation during LASSO regression (Fig. 5A). Under the condition of λ.1se, a total of 16 candidate genes with non-zero regression coefficients were identified (Fig. 5B). Subsequently, RF was employed to evaluate the relative importance of each candidate gene in constructing the classification model. Among the top 20 genes, NEIL1, NOTCH1, and FABP5 exhibited the highest importance scores (Fig. 5C-D). By integrating the results of LASSO and RF analyses, 8 overlapping genes were obtained (Fig. 5E): NEIL1, NOTCH1, FABP5, BCYRN1, GPR27, MOCS3, ARHGAP31, and NLRP1. Comparative analysis between tumor and normal tissues was conducted to confirm gene expression patterns between tumor and normal tissues. All 8 genes showed significant differential expression (P < 0.001), with ARHGAP31, MOCS3, and NOTCH1 being significantly upregulated in tumor tissues (Fig. 5F), while the others were downregulated.

div.head: Construction and evaluation of glioma prognostic risk prediction model
div.p: To construct and evaluate a prognostic risk model for glioma, the 8 feature genes identified via LASSO regression and RF were subjected to multivariate Cox regression analysis, using overall survival as the dependent variable. Among them, 6 genes (ARHGAP31, BCYRN1, FABP5, GPR27, NEIL1, and NOTCH1) demonstrated significant prognostic relevance (Fig. 6A). An individualized risk score was derived from the regression coefficients of these key genes. Patients were classified into high-and low-risk subgroups according to the median risk score (0.906). The prognostic model (Table 1) was established using the following formula: Riskscore = (-0. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis indicated that patients in the highrisk group had markedly worse overall survival compared with those in the low-risk group (P < 0.001, Fig. 6B). To further evaluate model performance, ROC curves were plotted. The AUC values of all 6 genes were close to 1.0, indicating exceptionally high predictive accuracy (Fig. 6C). A nomogram was constructed based on the 6 key genes to visualize the contribution of each factor to patient survival (Fig. 6D). Calibration curves demonstrated a close match between predicted and observed survival probabilities at 1-, 2-, and 2.5-year time points, confirming the model's reliability (Fig. 6E). Finally, validation using an independent CGGA cohort of 325 glioma cases further supported the robustness of the model. Consistently, Kaplan-Meier analysis confirmed that the high-risk group experienced significantly reduced median survival relative to the low-risk group (Fig. 6F), supporting the robustness and clinical potential of this prognostic risk score model in glioma.

div.head: NEIL1 promotes proliferation, migration, and invasion of U251 MG cells
div.p: NEIL1 is capable of initiating base excision repair (BER), a process highly relevant to the anticancer mechanism of TMZ. Therefore, NEIL1 was selected as a target gene for functional investigation. First, the expression levels of NEIL1 in U251 MG/TMZ (TMZ-resistant) and U251 MG (parental) cells were examined using qRT-PCR (Fig. 7A). Analysis indicated that TMZ-resistant cells exhibited a notable upregulation of NEIL1 (P < 0.001), suggesting its potential involvement in TMZ resistance. Subsequently, U251 cells were subjected to lentiviral-mediated knockdown (NEIL1KD) and overexpression (NEIL1OE) of NEIL1. qRT-PCR results confirmed that NEIL1 expression was significantly downregulated in NEIL1KD cells and upregulated in NEIL1OE cells (P < 0.01), indicating successful lentiviral transduction (Fig. 7B).

To investigate the role of NEIL1 in cellular functions, U251 MG cells were infected with NEIL1 NC (negative control), NEIL1 KD , and NEIL1 •E lentiviruses, respectively. CCK-8 cell viability assays demonstrated that NEIL1 •E significantly increased cell viability, while NEIL1 KD caused a significant inhibition of proliferation (P < 0.05, Fig. 7C). EdU staining confirmed that NEIL1 •E increased the proportion of EdU-positive cells, while NEIL1 KD produced the opposite effect (P < 0.001, Fig. 7D), indicating that NEIL1 promotes DNA synthesis and proliferation. Wound healing assays demonstrated that NEIL1 •E significantly enhanced the migratory capacity of U251 cells, whereas NEIL1 KD inhibited migration (Fig. 7E). Similarly, Transwell invasion assays revealed that NEIL1 •E promoted invasion, in contrast to the reduction observed in NEIL1 KD (Fig. 7F). Collectively, these results demonstrate that NEIL1 exerts protumorigenic effects in U251 MG glioma cells by promoting proliferation, migration, and invasion, suggesting that NEIL1 may function as a malignancy-associated factor in glioma progression.

div.head: TX16 reverses the pro-tumorigenic effects of NEIL1 overexpression in U251 MG cells
div.p: Although NEIL1 was shown to promote U251 MG cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, it remained unclear whether these effects were dependent on its enzymatic activity. TX16, an irreversible inhibitor of NEIL1 [35], was used in NEIL1 •E cells to assess this dependency. EdU staining demonstrated a significant increase in EdU-positive cells in the NEIL1 •E group (P < 0.01), confirming enhanced proliferation. However, co-treatment with TX16 significantly reduced the EdU-positive rate to below control levels (Fig. 8A). Wound healing assays indicated a significant increase in migration distance and rate in NEIL1 •E cells after 24 h (P < 0.05), while TX16 treatment notably suppressed this enhancement (Fig. 8B). Transwell assays revealed that NEIL1 overexpression promoted cell invasion, which was significantly inhibited by TX16 co-treatment (Fig. 8C). These findings suggest that TX16 can effectively reverse the pro-proliferative, pro-migratory, and pro-invasive effects of NEIL1 overexpression, indicating that TX16 exerts anti-glioma activity through inhibition of NEIL1 and may hold potential as a targeted therapeutic agent.

div.head: In vivo validation of NEIL1-Mediated glioma progression and reversal by TX16
div.p: To assess whether the pro-tumorigenic effect of NEIL1 observed in vitro also exists in vivo, we employed a subcutaneous xenograft model. NEIL1 •D significantly accelerated tumor growth and increased tumor volume (P < 0.01), while co-treatment with TX16 substantially suppressed this effect (Fig. 9A-B). TUNEL staining indicated that the NEIL1 •E group had a lower apoptotic rate than the control group, although the difference was not significant, whereas a significant elevation in apoptosis was observed in the NEIL1 •E +TX16 group (Fig. 9C-D). Ki67 staining showed markedly increased positive expression in the NEIL1 •E group compared to control (P < 0.001), which was significantly decreased following TX16 co-treatment (Fig. 9C, E). These results confirm the tumor-promoting role of NEIL1 in vivo and demonstrate the suppressive effect of TX16 on tumor growth and cell proliferation

div.head: NEIL1 enhances TMZ resistance in glioma
div.p: Previous analysis revealed that NEIL1 was highly expressed in TMZresistant U251 MG/TMZ cells. To investigate whether NEIL1 is involved in TMZ resistance, further intervention experiments were conducted. Compared with the Ctrl+TMZ group, NEIL1 overexpression significantly increased cell survival and IC₅₀ values under TMZ treatment (P < 0.05), suggesting enhanced TMZ tolerance. Co-treatment with TX16 significantly reduced both survival and IC₅₀, reversing the NEIL1-mediated resistance phenotype (Fig. 10A-B). TUNEL staining revealed that TMZ treatment markedly increased apoptosis in U251 MG cells (P < 0.0001, Fig. 10C-D), while NEIL1 overexpression significantly attenuated this effect. TX16 co-treatment restored apoptosis levels, indicating that TX16 may counteract the anti-apoptotic function of NEIL1. Furthermore, ROS staining demonstrated that NEIL1 overexpression reduced TMZ-induced ROS accumulation (P < 0.01), whereas TX16 restored ROS levels (Fig. 10E-F). These findings suggest that TX16 may restore TMZ sensitivity by inhibiting NEIL1-mediated suppression of oxidative stress.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: In this study, six key genes were identified through analysis of publicly available datasets, among which NEIL1 was selected for further investigation. The results demonstrated that NEIL1 overexpression significantly promoted proliferation, migration, and invasion of U251 MG cells. Moreover, NEIL1 was found to be highly expressed in TMZresistant U251 MG/TMZ cells, and its overexpression reduced ROS levels, thereby diminishing the cytotoxicity of TMZ.

It is well established that O⁶-alkylguanine repair mediated by MGMT is the primary determinant of TMZ resistance, however, this mechanism does not account for resistance in all patients [36,37]. Therefore, it is important to explore other mechanisms of TMZ resistance. It is worth noting that although NEIL1 and MGMT are both DNA repair proteins, they function through distinct pathways. Unlike MGMT, which specifically targets O 6 -alkylguanine lesions on DNA, NEIL1 is one of the initiating glycosylases in the base excision repair (BER) pathway. NEIL1 primarily removes various damaged bases, such as those caused by oxidative stress or alkylation, induced by ROS, thereby functioning in both nuclear DNA and mitochondrial DNA [38]. In addition, existing evidence shows that NEIL1 is significantly induced and up-regulated during oxidative stress [39,40]. Our study revealed that NEIL1 was enriched in PI3K-Akt, cAMP, and AGE-RAGE, all of which are upstream regulators of glucose metabolism and play essential roles in energy homeostasis [41][42][43][44]. Therefore, it is plausible that NEIL1 may affect cellular energy supply through these pathways, thereby activating metabolic signals that support enhanced cellular motility and invasiveness. Notably, in our experiments, the application of TX16 (a 2-thioxanthine derivative with NEIL1-inhibitory activity) reversed the pro-tumorigenic phenotype induced by NEIL1 overexpression, providing additional evidence for the essential role of NEIL1 in this regulatory process.

Furthermore, NEIL1 not only influenced cellular behavior but also contributed to TMZ resistance in U251 MG cells. Previous studies have shown that NEIL1 overexpression upregulates Bcl-2 and suppresses the caspase-9 pathway, thereby enhancing anti-apoptotic activity and ROS resistance, while NEIL1 knockdown produces the opposite effect [45,46]. These findings support a role for NEIL1 in protecting cells against oxidative damage and preventing excessive stress responses. One hallmark of TMZ resistance in glioma cells is the reduced release of ROS upon TMZ treatment. In resistant cells, TMZ fails to elevate cytosolic ROS levels, thereby diminishing its cytotoxic efficacy [23,47]. Our results showed that NEIL1 overexpression significantly attenuated TMZ-induced ROS accumulation, indicating a reduction in oxidative stress. Concurrently, DNA damage was mitigated (as evidenced by reduced TUNEL positivity), and apoptosis rates declined, collectively enhancing resistance. Co-treatment with TX16 reversed this resistance phenotype, suggesting that NEIL1 inhibition may hold therapeutic value in combination treatment strategies for glioma [48].

Despite the promising findings, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, this study was primarily based on bioinformatics and prognostic analyses, and some discrepancies between computational predictions and experimental results were observed. This may be attributable to differences in sample origin. Our dataset was derived from low-grade glioma, whereas U251 MG cells are derived from glioblastoma, a high-grade glioma. The two subtypes may differ in molecular mechanisms and phenotypic behaviors. This discrepancy prompts further consideration of whether NEIL1 and ROS play distinct roles in LGG and HGG.

Although NEIL1 was initially identified through a glycolipid metabolism-related gene set and shown to be enriched in multiple metabolism-related signaling pathways, we have not yet systematically investigated its specific regulatory effects on glycolysis or lipid metabolism at the experimental level. Previous studies have shown that NEIL1-knockout mice develop severe obesity, insulin resistance, and other typical features of metabolic syndrome as they age, suggesting that NEIL1 plays an essential role in maintaining metabolic homeostasis [49,50]. Therefore, the translational potential of NEIL1 in clinical practice still requires further investigation to fully elucidate its impact on human metabolism. Additionally, the TX16 used in this study lacks data such as pharmacokinetics, and therefore its clinical translational potential cannot yet be evaluated.

Future research will aim to incorporate metabolomic profiling, glycolytic flux assays, and expression analyses of metabolic enzymes to elucidate whether NEIL1 modulates metabolic homeostasis to mitigate oxidative stress and enhance TMZ resistance. These efforts will help refine our proposed regulatory axis: "NEIL1-metabolic reprogramming-ROS clearance-resistance enhancement.".

In summary, our results systematically elucidated the functional involvement of NEIL1 in glioma cells and TMZ resistance. NEIL1 overexpression was found to significantly promote the proliferation, migration, and invasion of U251 MG cells. In addition, NEIL1 reduced the accumulation of ROS, and alleviated DNA damage, thereby enhancing chemoresistance. These findings reveal a novel function of NEIL1 in glioma TMZ resistance.
